set1.q: Which condition belongs in the differential of subacute cardiac tamponade?
opts: Aortic dissection is on the acute tamponade differential, with myocardial infarction and massive pulmonary embolism.
Massive pulmonary embolism mimics acute tamponade by overloading the right ventricle.
Myocardial infarction with right ventricular involvement mimics acute tamponade.
Correct. Subacute tamponade is mimicked by constrictive pericarditis, congestive heart failure and cirrhosis, slower processes that also cause congestion.

set1.q: What is the Kussmaul sign?
opts: Systolic pressure falls over 10 mmHg on inspiration
A fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus, the hallmark of cardiac tamponade, not the Kussmaul sign.
A jugular venous pressure that falls on inspiration is the normal response. The Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical rise.
QRS amplitude alternates beat to beat
Alternating QRS amplitude is electrical alternans, seen in tamponade as the heart swings in the fluid. The Kussmaul sign is a jugular finding.
Correct. In constrictive pericarditis the jugular venous pressure is elevated and shows the Kussmaul sign: it increases during inspiration rather than decreasing as it normally would.

set1.q: Pericarditis that develops after a myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery carries which eponym?
opts: The Spodick sign is a downsloping segment between the T and P waves on the electrocardiogram of acute pericarditis. Post-infarction or post-surgical pericarditis is Dressler syndrome.

Correct. Pericarditis after myocardial infarction or after cardiotomy (cardiac surgery) is Dressler syndrome, typically appearing a few weeks after the injury as the damaged tissue inflames the pericardium.
The Beck triad is hypotension, distended jugular veins and muffled heart sounds, the classic picture of cardiac tamponade, not post-infarction pericarditis.
The Kussmaul sign is a jugular venous pressure that rises on inspiration, the classic finding of constrictive pericarditis, not an eponym for post-infarction pericarditis.

set1.q: Before committing to pericardiectomy, which test helps identify inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction?
opts: Transesophageal echocardiography images valves well but does not show pericardial edema or late gadolinium enhancement; cardiac magnetic resonance does.
A radiograph can show calcification of long-standing constriction but not reversible inflammation. Cardiac magnetic resonance identifies it.

Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance showing edema or late gadolinium enhancement identifies inflammatory, potentially reversible constriction before pericardiectomy, and it is now recommended for risk stratification.
A stress electrocardiogram looks for ischemia and says nothing about pericardial inflammation. Cardiac magnetic resonance shows edema and late enhancement.

set1.q: Which maneuver increases the intensity of a pericardial friction rub?
opts: Leaning forward while holding a breath

Correct. The rub gets louder with the patient leaning forward, holding a breath, and with firm pressure of the stethoscope diaphragm; holding the breath stills the lungs, so the sound must be pericardial.
Lying flat on the left side
The left lateral decubitus position brings out mitral sounds. A friction rub intensifies with leaning forward, breath-holding and firm diaphragm pressure.
Squatting changes preload and is used for outflow murmurs. The pericardial rub is brought out by leaning forward and holding a breath.
Light pressure with the stethoscope bell
The rub is best heard with the diaphragm pressed firmly, not the bell held lightly, and it intensifies with leaning forward and breath-holding.

set1.q: Which imaging helps evaluate pericardial thickness when constriction is suspected but unconfirmed?
opts: A ventilation-perfusion scan looks for embolism, and a plain film shows calcium in only a minority; neither measures pericardial thickness well.
Exercise treadmill test or stress echocardiogram
Stress testing looks for ischemia. Pericardial thickness is measured with cardiac magnetic resonance or computed tomography.
Liver imaging helps with cirrhosis, a differential, but does not measure the pericardium. Cardiac magnetic resonance or computed tomography does.
Cardiac magnetic resonance or computed tomography
Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance or computed tomography helps evaluate pericardial thickness, especially when the diagnosis is suspected but unconfirmed, and can show active inflammation.

set1.q: About what proportion of patients with acute pericarditis go on to recurrent pericarditis?
opts: One to five percent is much too low. Recurrence follows acute pericarditis in about 15 to 30% of patients, close to a third.
Correct. Recurrent pericarditis affects about 15 to 30% of patients with acute pericarditis, close to one in three, which is why adherence to the full treatment course matters.
Recurrence is common but not that common. About 15 to 30% of patients with acute pericarditis go on to have a recurrence.
Most patients do not recur. The recorded recurrence rate after acute pericarditis is about 15 to 30%.

set1.q: Which jugular venous waveform pattern is described in cardiac tamponade?
opts: Absent x descent, prominent y descent
This reverses the pattern. Tamponade gives a prominent x descent with an absent y descent.
Giant cannon a waves on every beat
Cannon a waves come from atria contracting against closed valves, as in atrioventricular dissociation, not tamponade.
Large v waves with each systole
Large v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation. Tamponade shows a prominent x and absent y descent.
Prominent x descent, absent y descent
Correct. In tamponade the venous waveform shows a prominent x descent and an absent y descent, because early diastolic filling is blocked by the fluid under pressure.

set1.q: How should all large pericardial effusions be followed?
opts: Correct. All large pericardial effusions should be followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms, alongside close follow-up with the specialty that matches the underlying cause.
An electrocardiogram cannot measure fluid. Large effusions are followed with serial transthoracic echocardiograms.
Catheterization is invasive and not used for follow-up of an effusion. Serial transthoracic echocardiograms are.
C-reactive protein tracks inflammation, not effusion size. Serial transthoracic echocardiograms follow large effusions.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set1.q: In the approach that uses C-reactive protein to guide therapy, when does tapering begin?
opts: Once symptom-free with a normal C-reactive protein
Correct. In the C-reactive protein approach, the level is checked at presentation and then weekly, and tapering starts when the patient is symptom-free and the C-reactive protein has normalized.
Once the friction rub can no longer be heard
Disappearance of the rub is not the tapering trigger. Tapering waits for both symptom resolution and a normal C-reactive protein in this approach.
After the electrocardiogram returns to normal
The electrocardiogram evolves over weeks and is not the tapering trigger. Symptom resolution plus a normalized C-reactive protein is.
Once C-reactive protein starts to fall, despite pain
A falling C-reactive protein is not enough while pain persists: tapering waits until the patient is symptom-free and the C-reactive protein has normalized.

set1.q: Which drugs are the anti-interleukin-1 agents used for recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Rituximab targets B cells and tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6; neither is the pericarditis agent. Anakinra and rilonacept block interleukin-1.
Azathioprine is a later-line immunosuppressant and colchicine is first-line therapy; neither blocks interleukin-1. Anakinra and rilonacept do.
Correct. Anakinra and rilonacept are the anti-interleukin-1 agents, now preferred for recurrent or colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent pericarditis with an inflammatory phenotype.
Infliximab and adalimumab block tumor necrosis factor, not interleukin-1, and are not named for pericarditis. Anakinra and rilonacept are.

set1.q: Which cardiac condition is a key mimic in the differential of constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Aortic stenosis causes an outflow murmur and exertional symptoms, not the constrictive mimic. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is.

Correct. The differential of constrictive pericarditis is subacute cardiac tamponade, restrictive cardiomyopathy and cirrhosis; natriuretic peptide is likely lower in constriction than in restrictive disease.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes outflow obstruction and a thick septum, not the fluid-overload, low-output picture that mimics constriction.
Infarction mimics acute pericarditis and acute tamponade. Constriction is mimicked by restrictive cardiomyopathy.

set1.q: Pericarditis symptoms persisting beyond which point earn the label chronic pericarditis?
opts: Two weeks still falls inside acute pericarditis, which lasts less than 4 to 6 weeks. Chronic pericarditis starts once symptoms persist beyond 3 months.
Persistence beyond 4 to 6 weeks without remission begins incessant pericarditis. The chronic label waits until symptoms have lasted more than 3 months.
Correct. Chronic pericarditis is when symptoms persist for more than 3 months; acute disease lasts under 4 to 6 weeks and incessant disease fills the gap up to 3 months.
No two-year threshold is used. Chronic pericarditis is defined by symptoms persisting for more than 3 months, after the incessant window closes.

set1.q: Which chest radiograph appearance suggests a large pericardial effusion?
opts: Correct. A large effusion enlarges the cardiac silhouette into a globular water-bottle shape, often with clear lung fields; at least 200 mL must accumulate before the silhouette enlarges.
Boot-shaped heart with an upturned apex
A boot-shaped heart is the classic film of tetralogy of Fallot, not of an effusion. An effusion gives a globular water-bottle silhouette.
An egg-on-a-string heart is transposition of the great arteries. A large effusion gives a water-bottle silhouette.
Bat-wing opacities are pulmonary edema; an effusion characteristically shows clear lung fields with a globular heart.

set1.q: What is the definitive treatment for established constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Pericardiocentesis drains fluid and is the definitive treatment for tamponade. A scarred, rigid pericardium must be removed surgically.
A medical trial of anti-inflammatories and diuretics for 2 to 3 months is reserved for early, stable constriction; established disease needs pericardiectomy.
The heart muscle is not the problem in constriction; removing the pericardium is. Pericardiectomy is the definitive treatment.
Correct. Constrictive pericarditis is often a surgical disease; pericardiectomy, surgical removal of part or most of the pericardium, is the definitive treatment and improves survival.

set1.q: Which is a recognized cause of cardiac tamponade?
opts: Correct. Causes of tamponade include acute pericarditis, iatrogenic injury, penetrating trauma, free-wall rupture after myocardial infarction, malignancy and aortic dissection.
Uncomplicated mitral valve prolapse is a valve problem that does not fill the pericardium. Free-wall rupture after infarction does.
Controlled hypertension does not cause tamponade. Free-wall rupture after infarction, trauma and malignancy do.
Stable angina is ischemia without rupture or bleeding. Free-wall rupture after infarction causes tamponade.

set1.q: In the symptom-based approach, tapering starts once the patient has been symptom-free for at least how long?
opts: One hour is too short to call a patient symptom-free. Tapering starts after at least 24 hours without symptoms.
Correct. When duration is based on symptom resolution alone, tapering starts once the patient has been symptom-free for at least 24 hours; the alternative adds C-reactive protein normalization.
Seven days is the window for judging response to therapy, not the symptom-free interval before tapering, which is at least 24 hours.
Four weeks overshoots. In the symptom-based approach tapering begins after at least 24 hours symptom-free.

set1.q: Which pericardial fluid studies are sent when tuberculosis is suspected?
opts: Gram stain and routine culture identify ordinary bacteria; mycobacteria need an acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture.
Antinuclear antibody is a blood test for lupus, not a fluid study for tuberculosis. Acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture are.
Correct. Pericardial fluid is sent for cell count and differential, Gram stain, bacterial and fungal culture, acid-fast bacilli stain with mycobacterial culture, and cytology.
Cytology to look for malignant cells
Cytology looks for malignant cells when cancer is suspected. Tuberculosis is sought with an acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture.

set1.q: Pericarditis symptoms that persist beyond 4 to 6 weeks, up to 3 months, without a sustained remission define which form?
opts: Correct. Incessant pericarditis is when symptoms persist for more than 4 to 6 weeks and up to 3 months without a sustained remission; past 3 months the label becomes chronic.
Recurrent pericarditis needs a symptom-free interval of 4 to 6 weeks or longer before symptoms return. Unbroken persistence up to 3 months is incessant pericarditis instead.
Chronic pericarditis is the label once symptoms persist for more than 3 months. Persistence from 4 to 6 weeks up to 3 months is called incessant.
Constrictive pericarditis is a structural diagnosis, fibrous scarring with loss of pericardial elasticity, not a time label. The persistent course described is incessant pericarditis.

set1.q: Failure to respond to a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug plus colchicine within 1 week suggests what?
opts: Normal recovery that simply needs time
Idiopathic or viral pericarditis usually improves within a week; no response by then is treatment failure and suggests another cause, not a normal slow recovery.
A drug allergy would show as a reaction such as rash, not as persistent pericarditis; failure to respond within a week points to another underlying cause.
Constriction that was missed at first
Constriction is a late occurrence with its own signs. Failure to respond within a week primarily suggests a non-idiopathic, non-viral cause.
A cause other than idiopathic or viral
Correct. Failure to respond within 1 week suggests a cause other than idiopathic or viral pericarditis, and no clinical improvement after 7 days of appropriately dosed therapy is a high-risk feature.

set1.q: Which tests screen for nephrotic syndrome as a cause of pericardial effusion?
opts: Correct. Albumin and urine protein screen for nephrotic syndrome, alongside thyroid tests for myxedema, rheumatologic tests, infectious serologies and a malignancy evaluation.
Thyroid function tests screen for myxedema, a different metabolic cause. Nephrotic syndrome is sought with albumin and urine protein.
The tuberculin skin test looks for tuberculosis. Nephrotic syndrome is screened with albumin and urine protein.
Cultures and lactate look for sepsis. Nephrotic syndrome is screened with albumin and urine protein.

set1.q: What is the median life expectancy with a symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion?
opts: Two to four weeks is shorter than reported. The median life expectancy is 2 to 4 months.
Correct. A symptomatic malignant pericardial effusion carries a limited life expectancy, median 2 to 4 months, and often recurs within that time, so palliative care is recommended.
Years overstates it considerably. The median is 2 to 4 months, with frequent recurrence.
A decade is not consistent with a symptomatic malignant effusion, which carries a median of 2 to 4 months.

set1.q: Which study is occasionally needed to confirm constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Correct. Coronary angiography with right heart catheterization is occasionally needed to confirm constrictive pericarditis, after echocardiography and cross-sectional imaging.
Biopsy of the myocardium is not the confirmatory study listed; hemodynamic catheterization with angiography is.
A bubble study looks for intracardiac shunts, not constrictive physiology. Right heart catheterization with angiography may be needed to confirm.
Troponin tracks myocardial injury and cannot confirm constriction. Right heart catheterization with angiography occasionally does.

set1.q: Which adverse effect of corticosteroids is a particular concern for older adults with pericarditis?
opts: Corticosteroids tend to raise blood glucose. The named concern in older adults is osteoporosis.
Correct. Corticosteroids increase osteoporosis risk, a particular concern in older adults on prolonged courses; bone health has to be considered when steroids replace an anti-inflammatory.
Bradycardia is not the corticosteroid concern named for older adults. Osteoporosis is.
Hearing loss is not a named steroid risk here. Corticosteroids increase the risk of osteoporosis.

set1.q: If pericardiectomy is planned, how should diuretics be used beforehand?
opts: Diuretics are not banned; they treat fluid overload in constriction. Before surgery they are simply used sparingly.
No route is prescribed for the preoperative period. The guidance is to use diuretics sparingly.
Correct. If surgery is planned, diuretics should be used sparingly in the preoperative period, even though they relieve the fluid overload of constriction.
Aggressive diuresis before pericardiectomy is advised against; diuretics are used sparingly in the preoperative period.

set1.q: Which situation calls for referral to cardiology in acute pericarditis?
opts: A first uncomplicated, low-risk episode is usually managed with medical therapy alone. Recurrence is a referral trigger.
Pain that eases after one dose
A brisk response to therapy needs no referral. Recurrence, nonresponse and constriction do.
A viral prodrome is the usual story of uncomplicated pericarditis. Cardiology referral is for recurrence, nonresponse or constriction.
Correct. Referral to cardiology is advised for no response to conservative management, for recurrences (recurrent pericarditis) and for development of constrictive pericarditis.

set1.q: Which electrocardiogram finding is fairly specific for cardiac tamponade?
opts: Axis deviation is not the tamponade sign. Electrical alternans, with low voltage, is.
Correct. Electrical alternans, alternating QRS amplitude, is fairly specific for cardiac tamponade, though it can rarely appear with very large effusions; low voltage and tachycardia accompany it.
Widespread PR depression with ST elevation is the electrocardiogram of acute pericarditis. Tamponade gives electrical alternans.
Peaked T waves suggest hyperkalemia. Electrical alternans is the fairly specific tamponade finding.

set1.q: Which patient should be considered for diagnostic pericardiocentesis?
opts: Most patients with acute pericarditis do not require an invasive workup. Diagnostic taps are for large, unexplained or suspicious effusions.
Any effusion found on a routine scan
Up to 6.5% of adults have an incidental effusion; finding one does not trigger a tap unless it is moderate to large and unexplained.

Correct. Diagnostic pericardiocentesis is considered during therapeutic drainage for tamponade, with high suspicion for neoplastic, purulent or tuberculous disease, or for a moderate-to-large effusion of unknown etiology.
Small effusion after a viral illness
A small effusion after a viral illness usually needs no tap; a simple effusion without compromise does not need drainage.

set1.q: Which feature predicts a poorer prognosis in acute pericarditis?
opts: Response within a week is reassuring; it is lack of response after 1 week that predicts a poorer prognosis, as does subacute onset.
Subacute onset over days to weeks
Correct. A subacute onset is among the poor-prognosis features, along with fever above 38, a large effusion, no response after 1 week, myopericarditis, trauma and oral anticoagulation.
Positional pain eased by sitting forward is the classic presentation and carries no adverse prognosis. A subacute onset does.
A preceding viral illness fits idiopathic or viral pericarditis, which usually does well. Subacute onset predicts a poorer outcome.

set1.q: Which bacterial cause of pericarditis is linked to rheumatic pancarditis?
opts: Mycoplasma is listed among bacterial causes of pericarditis but has no link to rheumatic fever; Streptococcus causes rheumatic pancarditis.
Histoplasma is a fungal cause of pericarditis. Rheumatic pancarditis follows streptococcal infection.
Correct. Among the bacterial causes, Streptococcus is tied to rheumatic pancarditis; the others listed are Staphylococcus, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Staphylococcus is a bacterial cause of purulent pericarditis but is not the organism of rheumatic pancarditis, which is Streptococcus.

set2.q: Which cancers are named for evaluation when malignancy may lie behind a pericardial effusion?
opts: Thyroid and kidney cancers are not the named examples. Breast and lung cancer are.
These are not the examples given. Breast and lung cancer are the named malignancies to evaluate.
Correct. When the cause is unclear, an evaluation for malignancy is considered, for example breast cancer or lung cancer, the cancers named in the effusion workup.
Prostate and bladder cancers are not the examples named. The workup considers breast and lung cancer.

set2.q: Which etiology accounts for more than half of cases of constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Prior radiation is a recognized cause with the worst survival, but it does not account for most cases. Idiopathic or viral disease does.
Post-surgical scarring is a cause of constriction, but more than half of cases are idiopathic or viral.
Connective tissue disease is one of the listed causes; the majority, more than half, are idiopathic or viral.
Correct. More than 50% of constrictive pericarditis is idiopathic or viral; other causes are post-cardiac surgery, prior radiation, post-infectious disease, connective tissue disease and uremia.

set2.q: Besides cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery, which service may an older adult need after a prolonged illness from pericardial disease?
opts: Nephrology joins the follow-up when uremia causes the pericardial disease. After a prolonged illness, older adults often need rehabilitation.
Infectious disease follows an infectious cause such as tuberculosis. After a prolonged illness and procedures, an older adult often needs rehabilitation.
Genetic counseling is not indicated for pericardial disease in older adults. Rehabilitation after prolonged illness is.

Correct. Older adults are more likely to need rehabilitation after prolonged illness, hospitalization and procedures; cardiology and cardiothoracic surgery cover imaging, pericardiocentesis and windows.

set2.q: Which pericardial fluid study is rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis?
opts: Acid-fast stain and mycobacterial culture are how tuberculous pericarditis is identified, a key diagnosis where tuberculosis is prevalent.
Gram stain and culture identify the organism and its sensitivities in purulent pericarditis, which guides antibiotic choice.
Cytology identifies malignant cells, an important cause of large effusions and tamponade, especially in older adults.
Correct. Cell count and differential are sent but are rarely helpful in establishing the diagnosis; Gram stain, cultures, acid-fast studies and cytology carry more weight.

set2.q: In a published African series of acute pericarditis, which cause accounted for most cases?
opts: Correct. Tuberculosis caused about 69.5% of acute pericarditis in the African series, against under 1% in Western Europe, where idiopathic disease (55%) dominated; think tuberculosis where it is prevalent.
Idiopathic disease made up 55% of the Western European series but only 13.7% of the African one, where tuberculosis caused about 69.5%.
Neoplastic causes were under a tenth of cases in both series. Tuberculosis dominated in Africa at about 69.5%.
Autoimmune causes were a small fraction in both series. In the African data tuberculosis accounted for about 69.5% of cases.

set2.q: Population data suggest a pericardial effusion may be present in up to what share of the general adult population?
opts: Half a percent understates it. Framingham data suggest up to 6.5% of the general adult population may carry a pericardial effusion.
Correct. Framingham cohort data suggest a pericardial effusion may be present in up to 6.5% of the general adult population, often small and unnoticed by the patient.
A quarter of adults is far too high. Up to 6.5% of the general adult population may have a pericardial effusion, by Framingham cohort data.
Forty percent is not the figure. The Framingham cohort suggests an effusion may be present in up to 6.5% of adults in the general population.

set2.q: Which imaging test is now recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis?
opts: A ventilation-perfusion scan looks for pulmonary embolism and has no role in stratifying pericarditis. Cardiac magnetic resonance does.
A chest radiograph is typically normal in pericarditis and cannot show active inflammation. Cardiac magnetic resonance can.
Correct. Cardiac magnetic resonance is recommended for risk stratification of complicated or recurrent pericarditis; edema or late gadolinium enhancement shows active inflammation.
Coronary angiography assesses the coronary arteries; with right heart catheterization it occasionally confirms constriction, but it does not stratify recurrent pericarditis.

set2.q: After drainage, what guides further management of a pericardial effusion?
opts: Correct. Further management of a pericardial effusion is whatever medical therapy the underlying etiology requires, such as treatment of cancer, tuberculosis or infection.
Colchicine treats pericarditis for set courses; it is not lifelong for every effusion. Management follows the underlying cause.
Pericardiectomy or a window is for recurrent or loculated effusions, not everyone. Management follows the underlying cause.
Anticoagulation is not a treatment for effusions; patients on anticoagulants are a higher-risk group. Treat the underlying cause.

set2.q: Which laboratory finding is often present in constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Raised sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
Correct. The inflammatory markers erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein are often elevated, while no natriuretic peptide threshold confirms or excludes the diagnosis.
A natriuretic peptide above a diagnostic cutoff
No B-type natriuretic peptide threshold confirms or excludes constriction; it is only likely lower than in restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Positive blood cultures in most patients
Blood cultures are not a feature of constriction, which is mostly idiopathic or viral scarring. Inflammatory markers are often elevated.
Low albumin with proteinuria points to nephrotic syndrome, a cause of effusion. Constriction often shows raised inflammatory markers.

set2.q: In the classic electrocardiogram evolution of acute pericarditis, what happens in stage 3?
opts: The tracing returns fully to normal
A return to a normal electrocardiogram is stage 4, the final stage. Stage 3 is T-wave inversion.

Correct. Stage 1 is widespread ST elevation with PR depression, stage 2 normalization of the ST segments with T-wave flattening, stage 3 inversion of the flattened T waves, and stage 4 a return to normal.
Widespread ST elevation with PR depression
Widespread ST elevation with PR depression and reciprocal changes in aVR is stage 1, the earliest stage.
ST segments normalize and T waves flatten
Normalization of the ST changes with generalized T-wave flattening is stage 2. Stage 3 is when those flattened T waves invert.

set2.q: Which chest pain pattern is classic for acute pericarditis?
opts: Burning, worse after meals and on lying down
Burning after meals points to esophagitis or reflux disease. Pericarditis pain is pleuritic and positional, eased by leaning forward.
Sharp, worse supine, eased by leaning forward
Correct. Patients typically have pleuritic (sharp) substernal chest pain that is worse supine and on inspiration and relieved by leaning forward: pericardial pain is pleuritic and positional.
Pressure-like, worse with exertion, eased by rest
Exertional pressure relieved by rest is angina pectoris, which must stay on the differential. Pericardial pain is sharp, positional and eased by leaning forward.
Tearing pain that radiates through to the back
Tearing pain to the back suggests aortic dissection, a rare differential. Pericarditis pain is sharp, worse lying down and better leaning forward.

set2.q: Which is a risk factor for multiple recurrences of pericarditis?
opts: severe late gadolinium enhancement predicts multiple recurrences; mild uptake is the reassuring end of that scale.
A prompt recovery from viral pericarditis is a good sign. An autoimmune etiology predicts multiple recurrences.
Correct. Risk factors for multiple recurrences are the magnitude of C-reactive protein elevation, the severity of pericardial late gadolinium enhancement and an autoimmune etiology.
It is a high C-reactive protein, by magnitude of elevation, that predicts multiple recurrences, not a low one.

set2.q: What adjustment is suggested for colchicine in older adults with pericarditis?
opts: Colchicine remains part of therapy; it is considered for dose reduction in older adults rather than avoided.
Colchicine is an oral drug and no intravenous route is suggested. The adjustment is a dose reduction.
Correct. Older adults call for caution with anti-inflammatory therapy, and colchicine should be considered for dose reduction, as it should for lower body weight.
Lengthening the course is not the adjustment. Colchicine is considered for dose reduction in older adults.

set2.q: Hoarseness with a large pericardial effusion comes from impingement of which structure?
opts: Hiccups can accompany a large effusion, but hoarseness comes from impingement of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which supplies the larynx.
Superior vena cava obstruction causes facial and arm swelling, not hoarseness. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is impinged.
The thoracic duct carries lymph and its injury causes chylothorax, not hoarseness. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is responsible.
Correct. Large effusions are associated with dysphagia, nausea, hiccups, cough and hoarseness, the hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement.

set2.q: What is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade?
opts: Correct. Expedient pericardiocentesis is the definitive treatment for cardiac tamponade; it is both therapeutic and an opportunity to send the fluid for diagnostic studies.
Anti-inflammatory therapy treats pericarditis but cannot relieve fluid under pressure. Tamponade needs expedient pericardiocentesis.
Intravenous fluids are a temporizing measure to support preload; they do not remove the fluid. Pericardiocentesis is definitive.
Diuretics lower preload and can precipitate collapse in tamponade. The definitive treatment is pericardiocentesis.

set2.q: At a second recurrence, low-to-moderate dose prednisone is reserved for which patients?
opts: Post-cardiac injury syndrome is grouped with idiopathic disease for the interleukin-1 blocker. Prednisone is reserved for systemic autoimmune disease.

Correct. At a second recurrence, an interleukin-1 blocker is added for idiopathic or post-cardiac injury disease that is colchicine-resistant with prior C-reactive protein elevation, while prednisone is for underlying systemic autoimmune disease.
Those with a typical viral prodrome
Idiopathic or presumed viral recurrence that is colchicine-resistant gets an interleukin-1 blocker, not prednisone, at a second recurrence.
Idiopathic recurrent disease with prior C-reactive protein elevation is where the interleukin-1 blocker is added. Prednisone is for systemic autoimmune disease.

set2.q: How does a small pericardial effusion typically present?
opts: Sharp pain eased by leaning forward
Sharp positional pain eased by leaning forward is the pain of acute pericarditis. A small effusion alone causes vague or no symptoms.
No symptoms or a vague, dull chest ache
Correct. A small effusion may be asymptomatic or cause vague symptoms: a dull ache in the chest, fatigue, decreased exercise tolerance or dyspnea.
Sudden hypotension with muffled heart sounds
Hypotension with muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins is the Beck triad of tamponade, not a small effusion.
Hoarseness, hiccups and dysphagia come from large effusions pressing on nearby structures. Small effusions are often silent.

set2.q: Which finding defines treatment failure in acute pericarditis?
opts: A friction rub that has faded
A fading rub can mean improvement, though a rub that becomes muted with new symptoms may mean fluid. Treatment failure is defined by persistent fever or pain, new effusion or worsening illness.
Mild fatigue after the pain resolved
Residual fatigue after the pain resolves is not treatment failure. Persistent fever or pleuritic pain, a new effusion or worsening illness is.
Normalizing ST segments are the expected electrocardiogram evolution (stage 2), not failure. A new pericardial effusion is a sign of treatment failure.
Correct. Treatment failure is persistence of fever, persistent pleuritic chest pain, a new pericardial effusion or worsening of general illness despite therapy.

set2.q: Which treatment addresses uremic pericarditis?
opts: Steroids are the underlying-cause therapy for autoimmune pericarditis. Uremic pericarditis is treated by correcting the uremia with dialysis.
Treating tuberculosis is the cause-directed therapy for tuberculous pericarditis. Uremic pericarditis needs dialysis to clear the uremia.
Pericardiectomy is the definitive operation for established constrictive pericarditis. Uremic pericarditis is managed by treating the uremia with dialysis.
Correct. Treating the underlying disorder is the rule, and for uremic pericarditis that means dialysis, alongside the usual anti-inflammatory approach and close renal follow-up.

set2.q: Which feature marks the inflammatory phenotype of recurrent pericarditis?
opts: Calcification is a sign of long-standing constrictive pericarditis, not of the inflammatory phenotype, which is high C-reactive protein, fever and imaging inflammation.
B-type natriuretic peptide is used in the constriction workup and does not define the inflammatory phenotype. A C-reactive protein above 10 mg/L does.

Correct. The inflammatory phenotype is a high C-reactive protein (above 10 mg/L), fever, and evidence of pericardial inflammation on imaging; these patients benefit from earlier anti-interleukin-1 therapy.
A normal C-reactive protein argues against the inflammatory phenotype, which is defined by a level above 10 mg/L, fever and imaging inflammation.

set2.q: After pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis, roughly what 5-year survival is reported?
opts: Twenty percent is closer to what untreated constriction might leave. After pericardiectomy, 5-year survival is nearly 80%.
Forty percent understates it. Five-year survival after pericardiectomy is nearly 80%, and 10-year nearly 60%.
Correct. Pericardiectomy gives a 5-year survival of nearly 80% and a 10-year survival of nearly 60%, whereas survival without treatment is low; earlier intervention improves outcomes.
Survival is good but not near-total; it is nearly 80% at 5 years and about 60% at 10 years.

set2.q: What does echocardiography usually show in uncomplicated acute pericarditis?
opts: A thickened pericardium with an abnormal septal bounce toward the left ventricle supports constrictive pericarditis, not uncomplicated acute disease.
Right ventricular diastolic collapse marks cardiac tamponade. Uncomplicated acute pericarditis often has a normal echocardiogram.
A ballooned apex with a normal base
Apical ballooning with a preserved base is stress cardiomyopathy. Uncomplicated pericarditis usually has a normal echocardiogram.
Normal unless there is an effusion
Correct. The echocardiogram is often normal unless there is an associated pericardial effusion, and the chest radiograph is typically normal; the diagnosis is primarily clinical.

set2.q: After a first recurrence of pericarditis, colchicine is typically continued for how long?
opts: Two weeks is far too short for colchicine after a recurrence; the course is 6 months or more.
About 3 months is the colchicine course for a first episode. After a recurrence, colchicine continues for 6 months or more.
Correct. A first recurrence is treated with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug until pain resolves and inflammatory markers normalize, plus colchicine for 6 months or more.
Colchicine is not given for life. After a first recurrence it is continued for 6 months or more.

set2.q: Which two groups of symptoms characterize constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Exertional syncope with an outflow murmur suggests aortic stenosis or obstructive cardiomyopathy. Constriction causes fluid overload and low output.
Fluid overload and low cardiac output
Correct. Symptoms come from fluid overload (peripheral edema, anasarca) and/or diminished cardiac output (fatigue, dyspnea on exertion), because the scarred pericardium limits filling.
Pleuritic pain and a friction rub
Sharp pleuritic pain with a friction rub is the picture of acute pericarditis. Constriction presents with fluid overload and low output, much like heart failure.
Fever with widespread ST elevation fits acute pericarditis. Constrictive disease gives nonspecific ST and T-wave changes with fluid overload and low output.

set2.q: Which echocardiogram finding supports constrictive pericarditis?
opts: Septal bounce toward the left ventricle

Correct. Typical echocardiographic features are increased pericardial thickness, abnormal septal motion or bounce toward the left ventricle, pronounced respiratory variation in filling and moderate biatrial enlargement.
Right ventricular diastolic collapse is the echocardiographic sign of tamponade, absent in an effusion alone, not of constriction.
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Constriction shows a thick pericardium and a septal bounce.
Apical ballooning with a preserved base is stress cardiomyopathy. Constriction shows a septal bounce and respiratory variation in filling.

set2.q: How often is the complete Beck triad present in cardiac tamponade?
opts: In only a minority of cases
Correct. The complete classic Beck triad (hypotension, dilated jugular veins, muffled heart sounds) is present in only a minority of cases, so its absence does not exclude tamponade.
The full triad is classic but uncommon; it appears in only a minority, so tamponade must be suspected without it.
Half overstates it. The complete triad is present in only a minority of patients with tamponade.
Chronicity does not decide it; slow effusions may stretch the sac and avoid tamponade. The full triad is seen in a minority of tamponade.

set2.q: Besides idiopathic disease, which etiology is singled out as especially important behind pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade?
opts: Correct. Neoplastic disease is an important underlying etiology, especially for pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade, so a large effusion should raise suspicion for cancer.
Coxsackievirus is a classic viral cause of pericarditis, usually after a viral illness, not the etiology singled out for large effusions and tamponade, which is malignancy.
Hypertension is not listed as a cause of pericardial disease. Malignancy is the etiology flagged for effusion and tamponade.
Hyperthyroidism is not a listed cause of effusion; the thyroid cause is hypothyroidism with myxedema. Malignancy is the etiology flagged for effusion and tamponade.

set2.q: Which is the most common disorder involving the pericardium?
opts: Correct. Pericardial disease presents as acute or recurrent pericarditis, effusion without major compromise, or a compressive syndrome, and acute pericarditis is the most common pericardial disorder.
Pericardial effusion is common enough to be found incidentally, but acute pericarditis is named as the most common disorder involving the pericardium.
Tamponade is uncommon, about 0.05% of hospital admissions in one large analysis. Acute pericarditis is the most common disorder of the pericardium.
Constrictive pericarditis is rare and its true population prevalence is unknown. Acute pericarditis is the most common pericardial disorder.

Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: Most pericardial disease is labeled idiopathic. What are most idiopathic cases thought to be?
opts: Malignancy is an important specific cause, especially of effusion and tamponade, but it is not what idiopathic cases are presumed to be; those are mostly viral.
Correct. Pericardial disease is most often idiopathic, and most idiopathic cases are likely viral; the specific virus is usually never isolated despite a preceding viral illness.
Autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis are specific etiologies, not the usual explanation for idiopathic cases, which are mostly viral.
Bacterial (purulent) pericarditis is an uncommon specific cause. The idiopathic majority is thought to be viral in origin.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pericardial disease: 2. Pericarditis 3. Acute 4. Recurrent 5. Constrictive pericarditis 6. Pericardial effusion 7. Cardiac tamponade
set2.q: What is the initial recommended therapy for most patients with acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis?
opts: Antibiotics have no role in idiopathic or viral pericarditis; they are for proven or suspected bacterial disease. First line is an anti-inflammatory plus colchicine.

Correct. A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (aspirin, ibuprofen or indomethacin) plus colchicine is the initial therapy for most patients, with gastrointestinal protection; prednisone replaces the anti-inflammatory only if it cannot be taken.
Prednisone plus a proton pump inhibitor
Prednisone is second line, for refractory cases or when nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs cannot be used, and it is given with colchicine. First line is an anti-inflammatory plus colchicine.
Anakinra plus colchicine from the outset
Anakinra, an anti-interleukin-1 agent, is reserved for recurrent, colchicine-resistant or steroid-dependent disease with an inflammatory phenotype, not a first episode.
